notes.scope: Two additional listening sets for APTIS Complete Trainer V3.2 and later compatible builds.
notes.l1_policy: 24 valid MCQ items per set, continuing sequentially after Set 04. Q103/Q122/Q138 omitted for visibly broken/non-English OCR; Q135/Q151 omitted because no generated-practice audio item exists. Raw source is preserved for every included item.
notes.display_cleaning: Only obvious display/OCR grammar artifacts are repaired in question_en; source_question_raw remains unchanged. Answer indices and source concepts are unchanged.
notes.l3_voice_compatibility: L3 script segments use M/F speaker labels and are compatible with the app gender-lock rule (Man=male voice, Woman=female voice even when Random voice is enabled).
notes.l4_shuffle_compatibility: L4 source answer_index remains canonical. The latest app shuffles displayed A/B/C each time L4 is reopened and maps scoring/key back to the source answer.
notes.provenance: L1 scripts, L3 dialogues, L4 monologues and L2 extra distractors are GENERATED_PRACTICE; source questions/answers/transcripts remain marked SOURCE.

L2.title: ENVIRONMENT PROBLEM
options: Does not use commercial cleaning products

speakers.speaker: A
speakers.script_text: "You know, it amazes me how much we throw away without thinking. I've started giving away my old clothes and furniture instead of dumping them. Think about it-someone else could really use what we consider junk. It's such a simple thing, but it keeps stuff out of landfills and helps people out. The more we share, the less we waste. Why let things rot in a corner when they could have a second life somewhere else? It makes me feel like I'm doing my part, even in small ways. Plus, it's a good reminder that what's old to me could be new to someone else."

key_vi.answer: Cho/tặng những đồ vật đã qua sử dụng
key_vi.explanation: Đáp án mục tiêu là “Give away used items”. Trong transcript, ý này được diễn đạt bằng các phrase throw away, giving away my, old, clothes. Khi nghe không chờ đúng nguyên văn đáp án; hãy nhận ra cụm đồng nghĩa/paraphrase.
key_vi.evidence_en: "You know, it amazes me how much we throw away without thinking.

speakers.speaker: B
speakers.script_text: "I think one of the biggest ways we can protect the environment is by changing what we buy. I only purchase products that are sustainably sourced or made from recycled materials. Every dollar we spend is like casting a vote for the kind of world we want. It's crazy how much waste and pollution come from manufacturing—choosing eco-friendly products is a way to push back against that. Sure, it might cost a bit more sometimes, but isn't the planet worth it? I mean, we talk a lot about big changes, but if everyone just started small, like switching to biodegradable packaging, we'd see a massive impact."

L4.title: 2 FAMOUS WRITERS
L4.script_text: People often have quick opinions about 2 famous writers, but my experience has been more complicated. At first I expected the most obvious explanation to be right, and I even considered the idea that they have always received considerable academic attention. Another possibility people often mention is that their works are mainly studied in universities. After looking at the situation more carefully, neither description really matched what happened. The better summary is that things were ignored. That difference matters because the speaker's final judgement is more qualified than the tempting alternatives. There is another aspect that is easy to miss. Some people argue that their works are easy for everyone to interpret, while others go almost to the opposite extreme and say that the ideas in their books are explained very directly. My own view sits elsewhere. What matters is significance. In other words, the conclusion depends on the exact conditions being discussed, not on a broad slogan. During the discussion I might use several words related to the wrong choices, because they are realistic possibilities. That does not make them the answer. The key is to notice when an idea is introduced only to be limited, corrected, or rejected. Expressions such as “however”, “in practice”, “actually”, and “what matters more” often signal that the speaker is moving toward the real position. For a listening task, I would therefore avoid selecting an option as soon as I hear familiar vocabulary. I would wait until the evaluation becomes clear, then match that meaning to the option that paraphrases it most accurately. The two ideas to retain from this talk are the ones expressed through ignored, academics and significance, difficult to determine; they represent the settled view rather than the rejected alternatives. A longer talk also includes background that may not directly answer either question. For example, a speaker may describe how the issue developed, mention another person's view, or give a small personal example before returning to the main judgement. Those details are useful context, but they should not replace the two target conclusions. When I practise, I try to separate background information from evaluation language. Background tells me what happened; evaluation tells me what the speaker finally thinks about it. I also listen for changes in certainty. Words such as 'probably', 'only', 'not always', 'unlikely', and 'depends' can completely change which option is accurate. If two answers share similar vocabulary, the safer choice is the one that matches the strength and direction of the speaker's final judgement.

options: They have both been overlooked by academics
They have always received considerable academic attention.
Their works are mainly studied in universities.

script_segments.speaker: M
script_segments.text: What makes this kind of discussion difficult is that sharing the same topic doesn't mean sharing the same judgement.

script_segments.speaker: F
script_segments.text: Exactly. A listener has to track who actually supports each idea, and whether the other speaker agrees, qualifies it, or rejects it.

script_segments.speaker: M
script_segments.text: Another thing I notice in discussions like this is that the same vocabulary can support different opinions. One person may mention the same problem as the other but use it to reach a different conclusion. That is why listening only for repeated nouns is risky; the important information is often in the verb, the evaluation, or the contrast that follows.

script_segments.speaker: F
script_segments.text: Yes, and agreement is not always expressed with the word 'agree'. Sometimes a speaker restates the idea positively, gives a supporting example, or says that something matches their own experience. Disagreement can also be indirect: a speaker may say 'perhaps', 'not always', or 'it depends', which weakens the claim rather than rejecting every part of it.

script_segments.speaker: M
script_segments.text: So during practice I would keep the four statements visible and make a quick mark only after each opinion becomes clear. If a speaker changes direction, the later qualified position should matter more than the first reaction.

script_segments.speaker: F

L4.title: REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT PLAN
L4.title_vi: Kế hoạch phát triển khu vực
L4.script_text: People often have quick opinions about regional development plan, but my experience has been more complicated. At first I expected the most obvious explanation to be right, and I even considered the idea that it provides many more alternatives to driving. Another possibility people often mention is that it strongly encourages people to stop using private cars. After looking at the situation more carefully, neither description really matched what happened. The better summary is that things were insufficient effort. That difference matters because the speaker's final judgement is more qualified than the tempting alternatives. There is another aspect that is easy to miss. Some people argue that the plan makes excellent use of all available land, while others go almost to the opposite extreme and say that most existing land is being used in the most efficient way. My own view sits elsewhere. What matters is available land. In other words, the conclusion depends on the exact conditions being discussed, not on a broad slogan. During the discussion I might use several words related to the wrong choices, because they are realistic possibilities. That does not make them the answer. The key is to notice when an idea is introduced only to be limited, corrected, or rejected. Expressions such as “however”, “in practice”, “actually”, and “what matters more” often signal that the speaker is moving toward the real position. For a listening task, I would therefore avoid selecting an option as soon as I hear familiar vocabulary. I would wait until the evaluation becomes clear, then match that meaning to the option that paraphrases it most accurately. The two ideas to retain from this talk are the ones expressed through insufficient effort, promote and available land, made good use of; they represent the settled view rather than the rejected alternatives. A longer talk also includes background that may not directly answer either question. For example, a speaker may describe how the issue developed, mention another person's view, or give a small personal example before returning to the main judgement. Those details are useful context, but they should not replace the two target conclusions. When I practise, I try to separate background information from evaluation language. Background tells me what happened; evaluation tells me what the speaker finally thinks about it. I also listen for changes in certainty. Words such as 'probably', 'only', 'not always', 'unlikely', and 'depends' can completely change which option is accurate. If two answers share similar vocabulary, the safer choice is the one that matches the strength and direction of the speaker's final judgement.

options: It doesn't do enough to promote alternatives to driving
It provides many more alternatives to driving.
It strongly encourages people to stop using private cars.
